output.reasoning: The task is real, bounded to the existing freeze-store subsystem, and almost all of its unusually extensive detail is load-bearing behavioral contract rather than implementation leakage. The repository already contains `TextFileBasedViolationStore` and its naming strategy interface, while the hidden suite directly verifies the stated integrity modes, classifications, safe-save behavior, ordering, and concurrency guarantees. However, the description unconditionally promises that every `description`-derived filename retains a whole 4–120-character word of letters or digits. output.reasoning:
The solution touches six files: four production files (`RuleDescriptionFileNames.java`, `RuleViolationFileNameStrategyFactory.java`, `StoreIntegrity.java`, and `TextFileBasedViolationStore.java`), one source user-guide file, and its synchronized generated HTML counterpart. All changes are task-related, and the production change comfortably exceeds the lane’s substantive-work floor.

The implementation traces the requested behavior end to end. Built-in naming selects random UUIDs by default or deterministic, bounded, ASCII-safe description-derived names with a readable whole-word prefix and a hash that distinguishes similar descriptions; reflective custom strategies are required to have public no-argument constructors, constructor-supplied strategies participate in both saves and relocation, and null/empty names are rejected before a mapping is inserted. Integrity mode parsing accepts only the three exact values. Initialization validates the index before opening it, performs `fail` inspection without mutating disk, requires update permission for `repair`, and serializes opening, examination, repair, and saves on the per-index `FileSyncedProperties` monitor.

`StoreIntegrity` gives shared identity precedence, including canonical/symbolic/hard-link identity, then classifies broken, resolved, colliding, misplaced, occupied, and unowned state. Repair only deletes or moves uniquely owned entries, follows a recorded link to its target for deletion/movement, preserves shared and unowned objects, and calls `apply` only when an index entry changed. Reports are deterministically sorted by condition and rule/file name. Save-time ownership checks reject the index and its aliases, paths outside the direct store folder, dangling/occupied names, and names recorded by another rule before inserting a new mapping; repair-mode empty saves retain the entry when deletion fails and preserve shared files. Description-permitted CR/LF cases are handled separately for integrity classification without changing ordinary embedded-carriage-return violation text.

The public store class, constructor, and strategy interface remain source-compatible, and the docs accurately describe the new settings. The configured Spotless unused-import gate and Java compatibility visible in the repository have no demonstrable violation. `verifySolution` reports all 42 baseline tests and all 137 new tests passing, including maintained concurrency and update-permission regressions; `solutionQuality` likewise found no code-quality or completeness defect. Static review found no uncovered concrete regression, unmet requirement, irrelevant change, or AI artifact.
output.summary: Clean, substantive implementation of filename strategies, integrity classification/repair/fail behavior, save safety, and in-process coordination, with relevant synchronized documentation and no grounded defects.

output.authorGuidance:
Clarify the filename promise so whole-word retention applies only when the rule description contains an ASCII letter-or-digit word of 4–120 characters. Then add four focused regressions: seed a legacy violation containing backslash followed by carriage return; assert both integrity examiners are still blocked before releasing an active save; configure `default.fileNames` through `Properties` defaults; and capture the exact CRLF-bearing description passed to a custom naming strategy.

The agent runs show that the task is hard for the intended reasons. Most unsuccessful implementations mishandled file identity through links, outside aliases, or aliases of the index, and one incorrectly tried to re-derive existing random names. Those are explicit parts of the contract, so the low pass rate is healthy rather than evidence of an unfair suite.

Keep the current harness, broad integrity matrix, baseline isolation, and reference implementation structure. The implementation’s ownership checks, deterministic reporting, effective-property handling, callback behavior, and synchronization are all solid; the needed changes are to the contradictory wording and the four coverage gaps, not the production solution.

output.reasoning: The harness is sound: it clears stale internal and advertised results, preserves native Gradle JUnit diagnostics, emits a conservative JUnit error with the Gradle log when build/collection produces no XML, validates malformed XML, atomically publishes one JUnit document, and forces failure when XML is absent or malformed. I found no platform/process leakage. Dynamic checks confirm all 42 selected baseline tests pass, all 137 new tests fail on base, all 137 pass with the reference, and six repeated base/solution runs were stable. The present assertions are fair and exceptionally broad, and repeated agent failures on shared/outside aliases track the prompt’s explicit shared-precedence rule rather than unfair expectations. However, an all-tests-passing legitimate run demonstrates three material false-positive gaps: it corrupts a pre-existing valid backslash-plus-carriage-return violation, normalizes the public filename-strategy callback input, and ignores an inherited default.fileNames conflict. In addition, the test specifically named as proving initialization waits for an active save never checks that either examiner remained blocked. Each omission has a prompt- or repo-grounded, reference-passing check and admits a realistic incomplete implementation.
